lines.text: **[VOSS BANK AG]{.underline}**
**[GMRA NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK]{.underline}**
**Collateral Trading & Legal --- Version 3.1**
**STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL --- INTERNAL USE ONLY**
**Prepared by:** Collateral Trading & Legal, Voss Bank AG, London Branch
**Approved by:** Henrik J. Lindqvist, Director --- Collateral Trading & Legal
**Version Date:** April 2025
**Supersedes:** Version 3.0 (September 2024)
**Distribution:**
> • Collateral Trading Desk (London Branch)
> • Legal (London & Zürich)
> • Credit Committee (Zürich)

This document contains proprietary negotiation strategies, approved credit parameters, and counterparty-specific commercial information. It must not be shared with, disclosed to, or made accessible to any external party, including counterparties, counterparty counsel, regulators (except upon formal regulatory request), or any other third party. Refer to Section 19 for the full confidentiality notice.
Right-click to update Table of Contents
**[Section 1 --- Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**
**[1.1 --- Purpose]{.underline}**

This playbook sets out Voss Bank AG\'s standard negotiation positions, approved fallback positions, and absolute walk-away thresholds for the negotiation of Global Master Repurchase Agreements under the 2011 ICMA form (with 2011 Annex I). It is intended to equip the Collateral Trading & Legal team at the London Branch (FCA FRN 487203) with authoritative guidance for each material commercial and legal term, enabling front-to-back consistency across all repo and reverse repo negotiations and ensuring that all agreed terms remain within parameters approved by the Credit Committee in Zürich.

The playbook serves several core functions. First, it provides the desk with a single, comprehensive reference document that eliminates the need for ad hoc consultation on routine negotiation points. Second, it establishes a clear escalation framework so that the desk and Legal know precisely when a counterparty proposal exceeds the authority delegated to the London Branch and must be referred to the Credit Committee. Third, it promotes institutional consistency --- ensuring that materially similar counterparties receive materially similar terms, and that departures from standard terms are documented and justified. Fourth, it reduces the risk of inadvertent agreement to terms that are incompatible with Voss Bank\'s regulatory obligations, including under FINMA\'s liquidity, capital, and large-exposure frameworks.
The following principles govern the application of this playbook:

> • This playbook is applicable to all GMRA negotiations conducted by or on behalf of Voss Bank AG, London Branch (LEI: 2138004WJZ83NHQKF744; CHE-314.827.059). For the avoidance of doubt, this includes negotiations where the London Branch acts through its appointed external counsel, Calder Stone Partners LLP, or through any other authorised legal adviser.

> • This playbook is not legal advice and does not override Credit Committee mandates issued on a counterparty-specific basis. Where a Credit Committee mandate imposes terms that differ from those set out in this playbook, the Credit Committee mandate prevails. The desk should annotate the relevant sections of this playbook to reflect any counterparty-specific mandates in effect.

> • Where a counterparty\'s regulatory status (e.g., SEC-registered broker-dealer, PRA/FCA-authorised firm, CFTC-registered swap dealer) creates specific structural requirements --- for example, with respect to the treatment of customer property under the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA), or with respect to margin segregation requirements under FCA CASS rules --- the desk must consult Calder Stone Partners LLP or internal Legal before deviating from the playbook positions stated herein. Regulatory-driven structural requirements may necessitate bespoke provisions that fall outside the standard terms addressed in this document.

> • Nothing in this playbook limits or modifies the obligation of the desk to comply with Voss Bank AG\'s broader compliance policies, including the Anti-Money Laundering and Sanctions Policy, the Market Abuse Policy, and the Conflicts of Interest Policy, each as in effect from time to time.
**[1.2 --- Scope of Application]{.underline}**
This playbook applies to the following instruments, structures, and settlement arrangements:

> • **2011 ICMA GMRA and Annex I elections.** The 2011 form is Voss Bank\'s standard master agreement for repurchase transactions. Voss Bank does not, as a matter of policy, negotiate under the 1995 ICMA GMRA or the 2000 TBMA/ISMA GMRA. If a counterparty proposes either legacy form, the desk should insist on migrating to the 2011 form. If the counterparty refuses, escalate to Legal.

> • **Bilateral and tri-party repo and reverse repo.** The playbook covers both bilateral structures (where collateral moves directly between the parties\' custodians or settlement accounts) and tri-party structures (including where BNY Meliora Trust Company, N.A. is appointed as tri-party custodian). The default structure under this playbook is bilateral; tri-party is elected only where specifically agreed and documented via a separate tri-party annexe.

> • **Buy/Sell Back transactions only where the Buy/Sell Back Annex is separately elected.** Buy/Sell Back treatment is not the default under this playbook. Where a counterparty specifically requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, to accommodate back-office systems that process Buy/Sell Back confirmations rather than classic repo confirmations --- the desk must refer the matter to Legal for negotiation of a separate Buy/Sell Back Annex. The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as part of the standard Annex I elections.

> • **Settlement through Clearstream Banking S.A.** (for Euro-denominated Eligible Collateral) **and The Depository Trust Company** (for USD-denominated Eligible Collateral). These are the standard settlement systems for the London Branch. Alternative settlement systems may be considered on a case-by-case basis, but any departure from these standard elections requires discussion with Operations (London) to confirm settlement capability.
**[1.3 --- How to Use This Playbook]{.underline}**
Each section below addresses a material commercial or legal term that arises in a typical GMRA negotiation. For each term, the playbook identifies three tiers of positioning:

> • **Preferred Position** --- the opening term Voss Bank will propose in a Turn 1 draft. This is the position that appears in Voss Bank\'s standard-form Annex I or in the initial mark-up of the counterparty\'s draft (where the counterparty circulates the first draft). The preferred position represents Voss Bank\'s optimal commercial and risk outcome. It is the starting point for all negotiations, and the desk should not concede the preferred position without first testing the counterparty\'s willingness to accept it.

> • **Fallback / Acceptable Range** --- the range of compromise the desk and Legal may agree without escalation to the Credit Committee. Within this range, the desk lead (at Director level) has full authority to agree terms on behalf of Voss Bank. The acceptable range is calibrated to reflect credit, regulatory, and market considerations, and to allow the desk sufficient flexibility to reach commercial agreement with a reasonable counterparty. Where the acceptable range is expressed as a numeric band (e.g., \$10,000,000 to \$25,000,000), any figure within the band --- including the endpoints --- may be agreed without escalation.

> • **Walk-Away Threshold** --- the point beyond which the term is unacceptable. Any counterparty proposal at or beyond this threshold requires escalation to the Credit Committee under Section 12 of this playbook. In certain cases, the walk-away threshold is absolute --- meaning that the Credit Committee itself is not authorised to approve a term beyond that point, and Voss Bank must either negotiate the counterparty away from its position or decline the transaction. In other cases, the walk-away threshold triggers a mandatory escalation, but the Credit Committee retains discretion to approve the term under exceptional circumstances.

The playbook also includes practical illustrations drawn from current or recent negotiations, particularly the ongoing negotiation with Meridian Capital Securities LLC (see Section 17 for a comprehensive counterparty-specific summary). These illustrations are intended to demonstrate how the playbook positions translate into real-world negotiation dynamics. They should not be treated as precedent for future negotiations with different counterparties, except to the extent that the underlying principles are of general application.
**[1.4 --- Current Active Negotiations]{.underline}**

This version of the playbook (Version 3.1) incorporates lessons from, and provides guidance specific to, the ongoing negotiation with **Meridian Capital Securities LLC** (CRD# 298417; EIN 83-2947561; LEI: 5493007XKBT49LP2QR12), a Delaware-organised SEC-registered broker-dealer. Meridian is a mid-tier US broker-dealer with a diversified secured funding business and an audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as at 31 December 2024.

The Meridian negotiation is at Turn 3 stage. Voss Bank circulated its Turn 1 draft on 14 March 2025. Meridian returned its Turn 2 redline on 28 March 2025, raising 23 individual mark-ups across the GMRA and Annex I. Of those 23 marks, 16 were non-commercial drafting changes and 7 were substantive commercial or legal proposals. Alistair Fenn of Calder Stone Partners LLP responded to 14 of the 23 marks by email on 4 April 2025, accepting 7 and providing Voss Bank\'s counter-position on the remaining 7. A call between Dana R. Castellano (Meridian\'s lead negotiator) and Henrik J. Lindqvist on 11 April 2025 resolved three of the outstanding commercial issues (sovereign haircut, corporate haircut, and margin threshold). Rachel S. Okonkwo of Pryor, Ashworth & Gelb LLP (PAG) memorialised the call resolutions by email on 14 April 2025. Meridian\'s Turn 3 redline and updated issues list are due from PAG on 18 April 2025.

References to the Meridian negotiation are included as practical illustrations throughout this playbook. The counterparty-specific terms, issues tracker, and Annex I elections summary for Meridian are consolidated in Section 17.
**[Section 2 --- Base Currency, Transaction Types, and Netting]{.underline}**
**[2.1 --- Base Currency]{.underline}**

The Base Currency for all GMRA negotiations conducted by the London Branch is **USD**. This is both the preferred and the mandatory election. The desk does not have authority to agree a Base Currency other than USD without Credit Committee approval.

All haircut calculations, margin thresholds, exposure caps, cross-default thresholds, and any other monetary amounts specified in the GMRA or Annex I are denominated in USD unless otherwise stated. Where a Transaction involves non-USD Purchased Securities (e.g., Euro-denominated sovereign bonds), the relevant amounts are converted to USD at the applicable spot rate for the purposes of margin calculations, exposure monitoring, and threshold comparisons.

The selection of USD as the mandatory Base Currency reflects the London Branch\'s primary funding activities in USD-denominated repo markets and ensures consistency with the Branch\'s internal risk management systems, which are calibrated to USD exposures.
**[2.2 --- Buy/Sell Back Transactions]{.underline}**

The default election for Buy/Sell Back Transactions under the GMRA is **Not Applicable**. This means that the Buy/Sell Back Annex (ICMA form) is not incorporated into the GMRA as a default matter, and no Transaction entered into under the GMRA will be treated as a Buy/Sell Back Transaction unless the parties have separately agreed and executed a Buy/Sell Back Annex.

Where a counterparty requests Buy/Sell Back treatment --- for example, because the counterparty\'s back-office systems are configured to process Buy/Sell Back confirmations, or because the counterparty\'s internal legal framework treats Buy/Sell Back Transactions differently from classic repos for tax or accounting purposes --- the desk must escalate to Legal. Legal will assess whether the Buy/Sell Back Annex can be incorporated without adverse effects on Voss Bank\'s netting, HQLA, or capital treatment, and will negotiate any necessary amendments to the standard Buy/Sell Back Annex.

The desk should not agree to Buy/Sell Back treatment as a standard Annex I election. The structural differences between classic repo and Buy/Sell Back --- particularly with respect to the treatment of income payments and the mechanics of close-out --- warrant separate and careful consideration.
**[2.3 --- Agency Transactions]{.underline}**

The default election for Agency Transactions is **Not Applicable**. Voss Bank AG, London Branch, transacts solely as principal in all repo and reverse repo transactions. The London Branch does not act as agent for any other entity, and it does not accept counterparties acting in an agency capacity unless the underlying principal is separately identified, credit-approved, and documented.

If a counterparty proposes that it will act as agent for an undisclosed or disclosed principal, the desk must immediately escalate to Legal and the Credit Committee. Agency structures introduce additional credit, legal, and regulatory risks, including questions of counterparty identification for AML/KYC purposes, the applicability of close-out netting opinions, and the treatment of the agency relationship under SIPA (for US broker-dealers) or the FCA\'s client asset rules (for UK-authorised firms).
**[2.4 --- Netting]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred election is that **Paragraph 7(b) of the GMRA is elected**. Paragraph 7(b) provides for the netting of payment obligations arising under Transactions on the same settlement date and in the same currency. This netting mechanism reduces settlement risk by minimising the number and gross value of payment flows between the parties on any given day.

Netting applies on a **same-currency, same-settlement-date basis** only. The desk must resist any counterparty attempt to broaden the netting scope to include cross-currency netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations denominated in different currencies) or cross-settlement-date netting (i.e., netting of payment obligations falling due on different settlement dates). Cross-currency and cross-settlement-date netting introduce additional complexities, including FX conversion risk, timing mismatch risk, and potential inconsistencies with close-out netting opinions. Any proposal to broaden netting beyond the same-currency, same-settlement-date framework requires Credit Committee approval.

For the avoidance of doubt, the netting election under Paragraph 7(b) is distinct from the close-out netting provisions that apply upon an Event of Default or termination of the GMRA. Close-out netting is addressed in the body of the GMRA (Paragraph 10) and is not subject to election under Annex I. The enforceability of close-out netting is addressed in Section 15.1 of this playbook.
**[Section 3 --- Haircuts by Collateral Type]{.underline}**

Haircuts are among the most commercially significant terms in any GMRA negotiation. The haircut determines the relationship between the Market Value of the Purchased Securities and the Purchase Price, and thereby establishes the degree of overcollateralisation that protects Voss Bank (as Buyer) against a decline in the value of the collateral between margin call dates. Haircuts also have direct regulatory consequences: haircuts that are too low may cause received collateral to fall below the thresholds required for HQLA classification or may result in higher capital charges under the Basel III standardised approach for securities financing transactions.

The haircuts set out below apply to the initial calculation of Purchase Price. They are not intended to replace or limit the ongoing margin maintenance provisions of the GMRA (including the Margin Ratio, if separately agreed), but rather to establish the baseline overcollateralisation at the inception of each Transaction.
**[3.1 --- Sovereign Collateral]{.underline}**
**Parameter**                       **Position**
**Preferred Haircut**               **2.0%**
**Minimum Acceptable**              **1.5%**
**Walk-Away**                       Below 1.5%

**Eligible Sovereign Issuers.** Sovereign collateral is limited to obligations of G7 nations only --- that is, the United States of America, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, the Federal Republic of Germany, the French Republic, Japan, Canada, and the Italian Republic. Obligations of sub-sovereign issuers (e.g., US states or municipalities, German Länder, Canadian provinces) are not eligible as sovereign collateral for the purposes of this playbook, even where such obligations carry an explicit sovereign guarantee. Sub-sovereign obligations may be considered as a separate collateral category on a case-by-case basis, subject to Credit Committee approval.

**Minimum Credit Quality.** Eligible sovereign obligations must be rated **A--** (S&P Global Ratings) / **A3** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better by at least one of those two agencies at the time of the relevant Transaction and continuously thereafter. If a sovereign issuer\'s credit rating falls below A-- / A3 during the term of a Transaction, the affected Purchased Securities cease to qualify as Eligible Collateral and must be substituted or the Transaction must be repriced. This requirement is implemented through the standard Eligible Collateral definition in Annex I, supplemented by Voss Bank\'s standard ratings-downgrade trigger clause.

**Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** The haircut is applied as a discount to Market Value to determine the Purchase Price. Specifically, the Purchase Price is calculated as the Market Value of the Purchased Securities divided by one plus the applicable haircut percentage (expressed as a decimal). This methodology ensures that the haircut operates as a true overcollateralisation buffer --- the Seller delivers securities with a Market Value that exceeds the cash advanced by the Buyer by the haircut percentage.

At the preferred 2.0% haircut, illustrative sovereign collateral with a Market Value of \$100,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$98,039,215.69** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.02). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,960,784.31, representing 2.0% of the Purchase Price.

At the minimum acceptable 1.5% haircut, the same collateral would produce a Purchase Price of **\$98,522,167.49** (\$100,000,000 ÷ 1.015). The overcollateralisation buffer narrows to \$1,477,832.51, representing 1.5% of the Purchase Price.

**Negotiation Dynamics.** For current negotiations (e.g., the Meridian negotiation), a midpoint of **1.75%** is within acceptable parameters and may be offered in a Turn 3 or later round as a commercial concession if the counterparty has proposed 1.5% and Voss Bank has opened at 2.0%. At the 1.75% midpoint, \$100,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$98,280,098.28**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,719,901.72.

The desk should be aware that sovereign haircuts below 2.0% are increasingly common in the interdealer market for G7 sovereign collateral, particularly for US Treasury securities and German Bunds. The preferred 2.0% position may meet resistance from sophisticated counterparties, and the desk should be prepared to move to the midpoint range relatively early in the negotiation in exchange for concessions on other commercial terms (e.g., margin threshold, cross-default threshold, or repricing frequency).
**[3.2 --- Corporate Collateral]{.underline}**
**Parameter**                       **Position**
**Preferred Haircut**               **5.0%**
**Minimum Acceptable**              **4.0%**
**Walk-Away**                       Below 3.5%

**Eligible Corporate Bonds.** Eligible corporate collateral consists of corporate bonds rated **BBB+** (S&P Global Ratings) / **Baa1** (Moody\'s Investors Service) or better, with a residual maturity of **10 years or less** at the time of the relevant Transaction. Bonds with a residual maturity exceeding 10 years are excluded due to their higher duration risk and greater sensitivity to interest rate movements, which increases the probability of a material decline in Market Value between margin call dates.

Convertible bonds, contingent convertible bonds (CoCos), subordinated debt instruments, and any instrument with equity-linked features are excluded from the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral regardless of credit rating or residual maturity. The desk should be vigilant for counterparty proposals that seek to broaden the definition of Eligible Corporate Collateral to include any such instruments.

**Haircut Application and Illustrative Calculations.** At the preferred 5.0% haircut, illustrative corporate collateral with a Market Value of \$50,000,000 produces a Purchase Price of **\$47,619,047.62** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.05). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,380,952.38.
At the minimum acceptable 4.0% haircut, the Purchase Price would be **\$48,076,923.08** (\$50,000,000 ÷ 1.04). The overcollateralisation buffer is \$1,923,076.92.

A counterparty counter of 3.5% sits at the extreme low end of Voss Bank\'s tolerance. The midpoint of 5.0% and 3.5% --- i.e., **4.25%** --- falls within the acceptable range and may be agreed without escalation. At 4.25%, \$50,000,000 Market Value yields a Purchase Price of **\$47,961,630.70**, and the overcollateralisation buffer is \$2,038,369.30.

**Walk-Away.** Haircuts below 3.5% are outside the acceptable range and constitute a walk-away unless the Credit Committee grants a specific counterparty exception pursuant to the escalation procedures set out in Section 12. The desk should note, however, that haircuts in the range of 3.5% to 4.0% fall within a \"grey zone\" --- they are technically within the walk-away boundary but below the minimum acceptable threshold. Any counterparty proposal in this grey zone must be escalated to the Credit Committee before agreement.
**[3.3 --- HQLA Eligibility Note]{.underline}**

The haircut levels set out in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 are calibrated to ensure that reverse repo collateral continues to qualify as Level 1 (sovereign) or Level 2A (eligible corporate) High-Quality Liquid Assets under the FINMA Liquidity Ordinance (LiqV) and the CRR delegated acts as applied via the Swiss \"equivalence\" framework. Maintenance of HQLA eligibility is critical to Voss Bank\'s compliance with the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) requirements imposed by FINMA.

The desk must not agree haircuts that would cause received collateral to fall below HQLA eligibility thresholds as periodically published by Treasury (Zürich). As of the date of this playbook, the current HQLA-floor haircuts are as follows:
> • **Level 1 sovereign collateral:** 0.5% minimum haircut.
> • **Level 2A corporate collateral:** 3.0% minimum haircut.

These floors represent the absolute regulatory minimum. The preferred and minimum acceptable haircuts stated in this playbook are intentionally set well above the HQLA floors to provide a margin of safety against regulatory reclassification. If a counterparty proposes haircuts that approach the HQLA floors --- even if the proposed haircut remains above the floor --- the desk must consult Treasury (Zürich) to confirm that the proposed level does not create adverse LCR or NSFR consequences.

Treasury (Zürich) updates the HQLA-floor haircuts at least semi-annually, or more frequently if there are material changes to the FINMA framework or to the CRR delegated acts. The desk should check the most recent Treasury circular before finalising haircut terms in any negotiation.
**[Section 4 --- Margin Thresholds]{.underline}**

The Margin Threshold determines the minimum aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess that must exist before either party is obligated to make or entitled to receive a margin transfer. A well-calibrated Margin Threshold reduces the operational burden of frequent small margin calls while ensuring that material exposure imbalances are promptly addressed. The Margin Threshold is distinct from the haircut (which establishes the initial overcollateralisation) and from the Net Exposure Cap (which limits the aggregate credit exposure to a single counterparty).
**[4.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred Margin Threshold is **\$250,000 symmetric** --- that is, the same threshold applies to margin calls made by either party (Buyer or Seller), and no transfer of Margin Securities or Cash Margin is required unless the aggregate Margin Deficit or Margin Excess, as applicable, exceeds \$250,000. This threshold is applied on an aggregate, cross-Transaction basis (i.e., it is calculated with reference to the net margin position across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA, not on a Transaction-by-Transaction basis).

The \$250,000 symmetric threshold is appropriate for the majority of Voss Bank\'s counterparties. It strikes a balance between operational efficiency (avoiding de minimis margin calls that consume settlement capacity without meaningfully reducing credit exposure) and risk management (ensuring that margin calls are triggered before exposure becomes material relative to the haircut buffer).
**[4.2 --- Acceptable Fallback --- Asymmetric Thresholds]{.underline}**

Where a counterparty (e.g., a regulated broker-dealer with net capital constraints, or a central bank with operational limitations on daily margin transfers) insists on a higher threshold for its own margin delivery obligations, Voss Bank may accept an **asymmetric** threshold structure. Under an asymmetric structure, the Margin Threshold for margin calls made by one party differs from the threshold for margin calls made by the other party.
Specifically, Voss Bank is prepared to accept the following asymmetric arrangement:

> • **Margin Threshold for Seller (counterparty) deliveries: up to \$500,000** --- acceptable provided that the **Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold remains at \$250,000**. Under this structure, the counterparty (as Seller) is not obligated to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin unless the aggregate Margin Deficit exceeds \$500,000, whereas Voss Bank (as Buyer) must return excess margin if the aggregate Margin Excess exceeds \$250,000.

> • This structure recognises that the counterparty bears a higher margining burden as Seller (because it is the party delivering margin in response to a margin deficit) while Voss Bank retains the benefit of a lower call threshold as Buyer (meaning that Voss Bank can call for margin at the \$250,000 level even though the counterparty cannot call for return of excess margin until the \$500,000 level is reached).

In the current Meridian negotiation, Meridian proposed \$500,000 symmetric at Turn 2. The acceptable resolution --- communicated to Meridian by Henrik J. Lindqvist on the 11 April 2025 call --- is to concede \$500,000 on Seller (Meridian) deliveries while holding the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold at \$250,000. This outcome is within the desk\'s delegated authority and does not require Credit Committee approval.
**[4.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**
The following positions are at or beyond the walk-away threshold:

> • Any threshold above **\$500,000** for either party requires Credit Committee approval. The desk does not have authority to agree a Margin Threshold in excess of \$500,000 for either the Buyer or the Seller.

> • Any proposal to raise the Buyer (Voss Bank) threshold above \$250,000 is presumptively unacceptable absent exceptional credit quality of the counterparty (e.g., a sovereign wealth fund or central bank with a AAA credit rating). Raising the Buyer threshold above \$250,000 reduces Voss Bank\'s ability to call for margin promptly and increases the risk that a material margin deficit will accumulate before a call can be made.

> • Any proposal to eliminate the Margin Threshold entirely (i.e., to set the threshold at zero) should be viewed with caution, even though it is ostensibly more protective of Voss Bank\'s interests. A zero threshold creates significant operational burden and may result in a high volume of de minimis margin calls that strain settlement capacity. If a counterparty proposes a zero threshold, the desk should propose \$250,000 symmetric as a more practical alternative.
**[4.4 --- Margin Call Mechanics]{.underline}**
In addition to the Margin Threshold, the following margin call mechanics are standard Annex I elections and should be included in all GMRA negotiations:
> • **Margin call cut-off time: 10:00 a.m. London time.** This is the time by which a margin call must be received by the recipient party in order to trigger a same-day settlement obligation.

> • **Calls received before cut-off: same-day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received before 10:00 a.m. London time on a business day, the responding party must deliver the required Margin Securities or Cash Margin on the same business day.

> • **Calls received at or after cut-off: next business day settlement.** If a valid margin call is received at or after 10:00 a.m. London time, the responding party\'s obligation to deliver Margin Securities or Cash Margin is deferred to the next business day.

The 10:00 a.m. London time cut-off is non-negotiable. It aligns with the London Branch\'s operational cycle and with the settlement windows of the Branch\'s primary settlement systems (Clearstream and DTC). Counterparty proposals to move the cut-off to a later time (e.g., 12:00 noon London time or 10:00 a.m. New York time) should be resisted. If the counterparty insists on a later cut-off, consult Operations (London) to confirm whether a later cut-off can be operationally accommodated before making any concession.
**[Section 5 --- Net Exposure Cap]{.underline}**
**[5.1 --- Standard Cap]{.underline}**

The Net Exposure Cap is the maximum aggregate net credit exposure that Voss Bank is prepared to accept to a single counterparty under the GMRA. It is set on a counterparty-by-counterparty basis by the Credit Committee in Zürich, based on the counterparty\'s credit profile, the nature and expected volume of the trading relationship, and Voss Bank\'s overall portfolio concentration limits.

For the Meridian Capital Securities LLC relationship, the approved Net Exposure Cap is **\$1,500,000,000** (one billion five hundred million US dollars). This cap was approved by the Credit Committee on 7 March 2025 as part of the pre-negotiation credit approval for the Meridian GMRA.

The Net Exposure Cap is expressed as a single aggregate figure and is not broken down by Transaction type, collateral type, or tenor. It applies to the aggregate net mark-to-market exposure across all outstanding Transactions under the GMRA at any point in time, after giving effect to haircuts and any margin transfers.
**[5.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**

The Net Exposure Cap is not typically a negotiated term in the traditional sense. It is a unilateral credit limit set by Voss Bank to reflect its own credit risk appetite, and it is inserted into Annex I as a Buyer election. The counterparty is free to set its own exposure cap (if any) on its side, and Voss Bank will not object to a counterparty\'s unilateral cap unless it is so low as to render the trading relationship commercially unviable.
The desk should be aware of, and resist, the following counterparty proposals relating to the Net Exposure Cap:

> • **Bilateral cap.** Some counterparties will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be bilateral --- i.e., that it apply equally to both parties, so that neither party\'s aggregate net exposure may exceed the stated cap. This is inappropriate because the cap reflects Voss Bank\'s credit assessment of the counterparty, not a mutual assessment. A bilateral cap would constrain Voss Bank\'s ability to manage its own exposure unilaterally. The desk should reject bilateral cap proposals.

> • **Indexation.** Some counterparties (particularly US broker-dealers) will propose that the Net Exposure Cap be indexed to the counterparty\'s own net capital or regulatory capital ratios --- for example, that the cap be set at a fixed percentage of the counterparty\'s excess net capital under SEC Rule 15c3-1. Indexation introduces variability and unpredictability into the cap and creates a risk that the cap will decrease at precisely the time when the counterparty\'s credit quality is deteriorating (and when Voss Bank most needs the protection of a firm cap). The desk should reject indexation proposals.

> • **Periodic review.** The Credit Committee reviews Net Exposure Caps as part of its regular credit review cycle (typically annually, or more frequently if triggered by a credit event). The desk may agree to include language in Annex I stating that the cap is \"subject to periodic review,\" provided that such language does not create any obligation on Voss Bank to increase the cap or any right of the counterparty to request an increase.
**[Section 6 --- Substitution of Collateral]{.underline}**
**[6.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred position on substitution of Purchased Securities is that the Seller\'s right to substitute collateral requires **prior written consent** of the Buyer (Voss Bank). Consent may be given or withheld in Buyer\'s sole and absolute discretion, and no obligation to act reasonably or in good faith shall apply to Buyer\'s exercise of the consent right.

This position ensures that Voss Bank can assess the HQLA eligibility, haircut adequacy, and concentration limits of any proposed substitute collateral before the substitution takes effect. It also preserves Voss Bank\'s ability to refuse substitution at times of market stress, when the quality and liquidity of substitute collateral may be difficult to assess in real time.

The desk should propose the prior-consent position in all Turn 1 drafts. Counterparties with active collateral management programmes will frequently resist this position, arguing that the consent requirement impedes their ability to optimise their collateral pools. The desk should be prepared for pushback and should use the prior-consent position as a negotiating lever --- conceding it in exchange for concessions on other terms, such as haircuts or margin thresholds.
**[6.2 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**

Voss Bank may accept a **no-consent** substitution framework --- that is, a framework under which the Seller may substitute Purchased Securities without obtaining Buyer\'s prior consent --- where all of the following conditions are satisfied simultaneously:

> \(a\) The Seller provides at least **1 business day\'s prior notice** to the Buyer of the proposed substitution, specifying the Purchased Securities to be withdrawn and the proposed substitute collateral in reasonable detail (including ISIN, nominal amount, Market Value, and credit rating).

> \(b\) The substitute collateral must be of the **same or better Eligible Collateral category** as the Purchased Securities being replaced. For these purposes, sovereign collateral may only be replaced with sovereign collateral of the same or better credit quality; corporate collateral may be replaced with sovereign collateral or with corporate collateral of the same or better credit rating and with the same or shorter residual maturity. A \"downgrade\" in collateral category --- for example, substituting corporate bonds for sovereign bonds, or lower-rated corporate bonds for higher-rated corporate bonds --- is not permitted under this framework.

> \(c\) At the time of the proposed substitution, there is **no outstanding Margin Deficit** in respect of any Transaction under the GMRA. If a Margin Deficit exists at the time of the proposed substitution, the Seller must first cure the Margin Deficit (by delivering additional Margin Securities or Cash Margin) before effecting the substitution.

If all three conditions are satisfied, no Buyer consent is required. The substitution may proceed upon expiry of the notice period, provided that the conditions remain satisfied at the time the substitution is effected.

This fallback was used to resolve the substitution issue in the Meridian negotiation at Turn 3. Meridian initially proposed a no-consent substitution right with no notice period and no quality constraints. Voss Bank countered with the prior-consent position. The fallback described above --- 1 business day notice, same-or-better quality, no Margin Deficit --- was proposed by Alistair Fenn of Calder Stone Partners LLP as a compromise, and was accepted by Meridian\'s counsel (Rachel S. Okonkwo of PAG) by email on 14 April 2025. This fallback is approved for general use in future negotiations.
**[6.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**
The following substitution rights are unacceptable and constitute a walk-away:

> • Any substitution right that permits a **downgrade in collateral quality** --- for example, substituting BBB-rated corporate bonds for A-rated corporate bonds, or substituting corporate bonds for sovereign bonds.

> • Any substitution right that permits substitution **during a Margin Deficit** --- this would allow the Seller to withdraw collateral at precisely the time when Voss Bank\'s exposure is already inadequately covered.

> • Any substitution right that does not require **at least 1 business day\'s prior notice** --- this would prevent Voss Bank from conducting even a basic assessment of the proposed substitute collateral before the substitution takes effect.

> • Any substitution right that permits substitution of collateral with a **residual maturity exceeding 10 years** (for corporate bonds) or with a credit rating below the minimum ratings thresholds specified in Sections 3.1 and 3.2.
**[Section 7 --- Repricing / Mini Close-Out]{.underline}**
**[7.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank elects a repricing / mini close-out option (commonly referred to as a \"repricing\" or \"re-rate\" provision) exercisable at the **90th calendar day** of any outstanding Transaction, or at each **quarterly anniversary** of the Purchase Date, whichever is later. The repricing right allows Voss Bank (as Buyer) to terminate and reprice the Transaction at the then-current Market Value of the Purchased Securities, adjusted for the applicable haircut, with the effect that the Purchase Price and Repurchase Price are reset to reflect current market conditions.

Exercise of the repricing right requires **2 business days\' prior written notice** to the Seller. Notice may be given by email to the Seller\'s designated notice address (as specified in Annex I) or by such other means as the parties may agree.
**[7.2 --- Rationale]{.underline}**

Repricing rights protect Voss Bank against cumulative drift in collateral value on term trades. In a term repo transaction, the Purchase Price is fixed at inception based on the Market Value of the Purchased Securities at that time, adjusted for the applicable haircut. Over the life of the trade, the Market Value of the Purchased Securities may change --- due to interest rate movements, credit spread widening or tightening, or other market factors --- while the Purchase Price remains fixed.

The margin maintenance provisions of the GMRA (Paragraph 4) provide some protection against collateral value decline by requiring the Seller to deliver additional margin when the Margin Deficit exceeds the Margin Threshold. However, margin calls alone may not fully cure mark-to-market exposure on long-dated term trades, particularly where:
> \(a\) the Margin Threshold is set at a level that allows a material margin deficit to accumulate before a call is triggered;
> \(b\) the frequency of mark-to-market valuation is limited (e.g., daily valuation may miss intra-day volatility spikes);
> \(c\) the collateral has declined in credit quality or liquidity to the point where its Market Value, even after margin top-ups, no longer provides adequate protection; or
> \(d\) the Seller is unable or unwilling to deliver margin in response to a call, creating a period of unhedged exposure before an Event of Default is triggered.

The repricing right addresses these risks by allowing Voss Bank to periodically \"reset\" the economics of the trade to current market conditions. In effect, the repricing operates as a mini close-out: the original Transaction is terminated, the net settlement amount is calculated, and a new Transaction is simultaneously entered into at current prices. This mechanism is particularly important for term trades with a duration exceeding 60 days, where the cumulative risk of collateral value drift is most acute.
**[7.3 --- Acceptable Fallback]{.underline}**

The preferred position --- repricing at the 90th calendar day or quarterly, whichever is later, with 2 business days\' prior notice --- is also the fallback minimum. Voss Bank does not have a broader fallback range for the repricing provision; the preferred position represents the minimum acceptable level of protection.

Voss Bank may accept a counterparty proposal that aligns with this formulation even if the counterparty characterises it as a compromise or a concession. For example, if the counterparty proposes \"repricing at quarterly intervals with 2 business days\' notice,\" this is substantively equivalent to the Voss Bank position (since quarterly repricing is consistent with the \"90th calendar day or quarterly, whichever is later\" formulation) and should be accepted.

The desk should note that the repricing right is exercisable at Voss Bank\'s option --- it is not an automatic repricing. Voss Bank is not obligated to exercise the repricing right at any particular interval. The right provides flexibility to reprice when market conditions warrant, without creating an obligation to reprice when conditions are stable.
**[7.4 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

**No repricing right at all is unacceptable for term trades with a duration exceeding 60 days.** This is a firm walk-away, and it applies regardless of the counterparty\'s credit quality or the haircut level agreed. The repricing right is a structural protection that is independent of, and complementary to, the haircut and margin maintenance provisions.

Any counterparty that deletes the repricing right entirely, or that confines the repricing right to maturity rolls only (effectively eliminating intra-term repricing), is proposing a position that falls outside Voss Bank\'s risk tolerance. The desk should not agree to such a proposal, even as a concession in exchange for favourable terms on other points.

In the Meridian negotiation, Meridian\'s Turn 2 redline effectively deleted repricing for in-term periods by proposing that repricing be available only at maturity roll --- that is, only when the original Transaction matures and the parties agree to roll the trade into a new Transaction. This was flagged as unacceptable by Calder Stone Partners LLP, and Alistair Fenn communicated a revised Voss Bank position to PAG by email on 4 April 2025. The revised position --- 90th day or quarterly, whichever is later, with 2 business days\' notice --- is within the acceptable range and should be accepted by Meridian at Turn 3.

If Meridian continues to resist the repricing right at Turn 3, the desk should escalate to Henrik J. Lindqvist for a direct conversation with Dana R. Castellano. The repricing right is a non-negotiable structural protection, and Voss Bank will not proceed with the Meridian GMRA without it.
**[Section 8 --- Cross-Default Threshold]{.underline}**
**[8.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred cross-default threshold is **\$10,000,000** (ten million US dollars). This represents the minimum amount of third-party indebtedness that, if subject to default, acceleration, or non-payment at maturity, triggers a cross-default Event of Default under the GMRA. The cross-default threshold applies to both parties (Buyer and Seller) and is intended to provide early warning of a counterparty\'s financial distress by capturing defaults on material third-party obligations.

A low cross-default threshold is consistent with Voss Bank\'s conservative credit risk management philosophy. By setting the threshold at \$10,000,000, Voss Bank ensures that relatively small defaults on third-party indebtedness --- which may be precursors to broader financial difficulty --- trigger the GMRA\'s Event of Default provisions and enable Voss Bank to exercise its close-out and liquidation rights before the counterparty\'s financial position deteriorates further.
**[8.2 --- Acceptable Range]{.underline}**
Voss Bank\'s acceptable range for the cross-default threshold is **\$10,000,000 to \$25,000,000**. Within this range, the desk may agree any figure without escalation to the Credit Committee.
The following considerations should inform the desk\'s calibration of the cross-default threshold within the acceptable range:

> • **Counterparty\'s net capital or regulatory capital.** A threshold of approximately 5--7% of audited net capital is a reasonable benchmark that ensures the cross-default provision is triggered by defaults that are material relative to the counterparty\'s financial resources, without being so low as to capture trivial or operational payment failures. For Meridian Capital Securities LLC (audited net capital of \$412,000,000 as at 31 December 2024), a \$25,000,000 threshold represents approximately 6.07% of net capital, which falls within the 5--7% benchmark range.

> • **Nature of the counterparty\'s other financial indebtedness.** Counterparties with large outstanding bond or loan portfolios may argue that a low cross-default threshold creates an unacceptable risk of a cascade of cross-acceleration events --- where a default under one agreement triggers cross-defaults under multiple other agreements, amplifying financial distress rather than providing early warning. This concern has some merit, and the desk should be prepared to move within the acceptable range to accommodate it.

> • **Likelihood of cross-acceleration cascades.** In markets subject to stress, a low cross-default threshold can itself contribute to systemic instability by triggering a chain of cross-defaults across multiple master agreements. The desk should consider whether the counterparty\'s overall cross-default architecture (across its ISDA Master Agreements, GMRAs, prime brokerage agreements, and other trading documentation) is consistent with the threshold proposed under this GMRA.
**[8.3 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**

Any cross-default threshold **above \$50,000,000** is a walk-away. At that level, the cross-default provision becomes commercially meaningless for a counterparty of Meridian\'s size and profile --- a \$50,000,000 default would represent only approximately 12.1% of Meridian\'s net capital, and a counterparty in that degree of distress would likely already have triggered other Events of Default (e.g., failure to pay, Act of Insolvency) before the cross-default threshold was reached.

Thresholds between \$25,000,001 and \$50,000,000 fall within the escalation band. The desk does not have authority to agree a threshold in this range without Credit Committee approval. The Credit Committee will assess whether the higher threshold is justified by the counterparty\'s credit profile, the nature of the trading relationship, and any risk-mitigating factors (e.g., the availability of additional collateral, the existence of a credit support annex, or the counterparty\'s agreement to enhanced reporting obligations).
**[8.4 --- Meridian Negotiation Status]{.underline}**
The cross-default threshold is one of the open commercial issues in the Meridian negotiation. The negotiation history is as follows:
> • **Voss Bank\'s Turn 1 and Turn 2 position:** \$10,000,000.
> • **Meridian\'s Turn 2 counter:** \$50,000,000 (at the walk-away boundary).
> • **Expected Meridian Turn 3 counter:** \$25,000,000 (the top of Voss Bank\'s acceptable range).

If Meridian comes back at \$25,000,000 in its Turn 3 redline, the desk is authorised to agree without escalation. This figure represents 6.07% of Meridian\'s audited net capital, which falls within the 5--7% benchmark range and is consistent with the cross-default thresholds agreed in comparable GMRA negotiations with US broker-dealers of similar size and credit profile.
If Meridian holds at \$50,000,000 or proposes a figure between \$25,000,001 and \$50,000,000, the desk must escalate to the Credit Committee pursuant to Section 12.
**[Section 9 --- Act of Insolvency Grace Period]{.underline}**
**[9.1 --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**

Voss Bank\'s preferred position is **zero days** --- any Act of Insolvency constitutes an immediate Event of Default with no cure or grace period. An Act of Insolvency is defined in the GMRA to include (among other things) the presentation of a winding-up petition, the appointment of an administrator, receiver, or trustee, the filing of a voluntary bankruptcy petition, and any analogous proceeding under the laws of the relevant jurisdiction.

The zero-day position reflects Voss Bank\'s view that any Act of Insolvency --- even a technical or involuntary filing --- creates an immediate and material risk to Voss Bank\'s ability to realise its collateral rights and to enforce close-out netting. In the US context, the commencement of SIPA proceedings against a broker-dealer can result in an immediate freeze on the firm\'s assets and trading activity, and any delay in triggering the GMRA\'s Event of Default provisions increases the risk that Voss Bank will be unable to close out its positions and liquidate collateral before the counterparty\'s assets are placed beyond reach.

The gross-up obligation ensures that the recipient party receives the full amount of each payment as if no tax had been withheld or deducted.
404: >
405: > • **Cure period for failure to gross up: 5 business days** from written notice by the aggrieved party to the defaulting party. Written notice must specify the payment in respect of which the gross-up obligation has not been satisfied, the amount of the shortfall, and the relevant tax jurisdiction.
406: >
407: > • **Failure to cure within the cure period constitutes an Event of Default.** If the defaulting party does not pay the gross-up amount within 5 business days of receipt of written notice, the failure constitutes an Event of Default under the GMRA, entitling the Non-Defaulting Party to exercise all remedies available under the GMRA, including close-out and liquidation of collateral.
408: 
409: **[10.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**
410: 
411: The 5 business day cure period is a firm position. The desk should resist counterparty attempts to extend the cure period beyond 5 business days. Common counterparty requests include:
412: 
413: > • **Extension to 10 or 15 business days.** Some counterparties argue that 5 business days is insufficient to investigate and resolve a tax gross-up failure, particularly where the failure results from an unexpected change in tax law or treaty interpretation. The desk should respond that the gross-up obligation is a strict obligation, and that the 5 business day cure period provides ample time for a party acting in good faith to remit the shortfall while it investigates the underlying tax issue. Investigation can continue after the cure payment is made.
414: >
415: > • **Carve-out for disputed amounts.** Some counterparties propose that the Event of Default trigger should not apply where the defaulting party disputes in good faith that a gross-up obligation exists (e.g., because it disputes the applicability of the relevant withholding tax). The desk should reject this proposal. Disputes over the applicability of withholding taxes should be resolved through the dispute resolution mechanism agreed under the GMRA (see Section 11), but the existence of a dispute should not suspend the defaulting party\'s obligation to make the gross-up payment pending resolution.
416: 
417: The tax gross-up obligation is bilateral --- it applies to both Buyer and Seller. This is appropriate because both parties may make payments under the GMRA that are subject to withholding or deduction for tax (e.g., Purchase Price payments by the Buyer, Repurchase Price payments by the Seller, manufactured income payments, and margin payments).
418: 
419: **[Section 11 --- Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**
420: 
421: **[11.1 --- Governing Law]{.underline}**
422: 
423: **English law is mandatory.** Voss Bank will not agree to New York law, Swiss law, or any other governing law for the GMRA. This position is non-negotiable and applies without exception, regardless of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction of organisation, the location of the Purchased Securities, or the currency of the Transactions.
424: 
425: The mandatory English law position reflects several considerations:
426: 
427: > • **FINMA guidance.** FINMA has issued guidance confirming the enforceability of close-out netting under English-law master agreements governed by the laws of England and Wales. Voss Bank\'s close-out netting opinions --- which underpin the capital treatment of its SFT portfolio --- are predicated on English governing law. A change in governing law would require new netting opinions and could potentially result in adverse capital treatment during the period between execution and receipt of those opinions.
428: >
429: > • **Market standard.** The 2011 ICMA GMRA is an English-law document by design, and the vast majority of GMRA negotiations in the European and cross-border markets are conducted on the basis of English governing law. Deviating from this standard would be unusual and would raise questions from regulators and auditors.
430: >
431: > • **Predictability and precedent.** English law offers a well-developed body of case law on the interpretation and enforcement of master agreement provisions, including close-out netting, haircut mechanics, and Event of Default triggers. This body of precedent provides a high degree of predictability in the event of a dispute.
432: 
433: The desk should be aware that US counterparties (including Meridian) may initially propose New York law, reflecting their familiarity with New York-law governed master agreements (particularly the ISDA Master Agreement and the MRA). The desk should explain that the GMRA is an English-law form and that Voss Bank\'s regulatory and capital framework requires English governing law. In the desk\'s experience, US counterparties typically accept English law once the rationale is explained.
434: 
435: **[11.2 --- Dispute Resolution --- Preferred Position]{.underline}**
436: 
437: Voss Bank\'s preferred dispute resolution mechanism is **LCIA arbitration**, seated in London, conducted under the LCIA Rules as in effect at the date of the GMRA. Key features of the preferred arbitration clause include:
438: 
439: > • **Seat of arbitration:** London, England.
440: >
441: > • **Number of arbitrators:** Three, unless the parties agree to a sole arbitrator.
442: >
443: > • **Language of arbitration:** English.
444: >
445: > • **Governing rules:** LCIA Arbitration Rules as in effect at the date of the GMRA.
446: 
447: LCIA arbitration is Voss Bank\'s preferred mechanism for two principal reasons:
448: 
449: > *Enforceability.* Arbitral awards rendered by an LCIA tribunal seated in London are enforceable in over 170 jurisdictions under the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards (1958). This is particularly important for US broker-dealer counterparties such as Meridian, where Voss Bank may need to enforce an award in the United States. While English court judgments are generally enforceable in the US under comity principles, the New York Convention provides a more streamlined and predictable enforcement mechanism.
450: >
451: > *Confidentiality.* LCIA arbitration proceedings are confidential by default under the LCIA Rules. Court proceedings, by contrast, are generally public. Confidentiality is important to Voss Bank because disputes under the GMRA may involve commercially sensitive information about Voss Bank\'s trading strategies, collateral positions, and credit exposures.
452: 
453: **[11.3 --- Dispute Resolution --- Acceptable Fallbacks]{.underline}**
454: 
455: Voss Bank is prepared to accept the following fallback dispute resolution mechanisms, in order of preference:
456: 
457: **Fallback 1: LCIA arbitration with expedited procedure.** Voss Bank may accept a counterparty request for the LCIA expedited procedure to apply to claims with a value of **£5,000,000 or \$5,000,000 or less**. The expedited procedure provides for a shortened timeline and a sole arbitrator (rather than a three-member tribunal), which reduces costs and accelerates resolution for smaller claims. This is a reasonable efficiency concession that does not compromise Voss Bank\'s substantive rights, and it is within the desk\'s authority to agree without escalation.
458: 
459: The expedited procedure threshold may be denominated in either GBP or USD, depending on the counterparty\'s preference. The desk should ensure that the threshold is clearly defined and that the expedited procedure applies only to the initial value of the claim as stated in the Request for Arbitration (not to the aggregate of claim and counterclaim, which could artificially bring a larger dispute within the expedited procedure).
460: 
461: **Fallback 2: English High Court (non-exclusive jurisdiction).** If the counterparty rejects LCIA arbitration entirely --- and only in that case --- Voss Bank may agree to the **non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of England and Wales**. Non-exclusive jurisdiction means that either party may commence proceedings in the English courts, but neither party is precluded from commencing proceedings in another court of competent jurisdiction.
462: 
463: **Exclusive jurisdiction is not acceptable.** Exclusive jurisdiction would prevent Voss Bank from commencing proceedings in other jurisdictions where enforcement may be more effective (e.g., the counterparty\'s home jurisdiction, or a jurisdiction where the counterparty\'s assets are located). The desk must reject any proposal for exclusive jurisdiction, whether of the English courts or of any other court.
464: 
465: **[11.4 --- Walk-Away]{.underline}**
466: 
467: The following dispute resolution positions are at or beyond the walk-away threshold:
468: 
469: > • **Any governing law other than English law.** This is an absolute walk-away, as discussed in Section 11.1.
470: >
471: > • **Exclusive jurisdiction of any court.** Whether English, New York, Swiss, or any other court --- exclusive jurisdiction is unacceptable.
472: >
473: > • **Arbitration seated outside London.** Voss Bank requires that any arbitration be seated in London. This ensures that the arbitration is governed by the English Arbitration Act 1996 and that the supervisory court for the arbitration is the English High Court. Arbitration seated in other jurisdictions (e.g., New York, Geneva, Singapore) is not acceptable, even if the arbitration is conducted under the LCIA Rules.
474: >
475: > • **Binding expert determination.** Some counterparties may propose binding expert determination for valuation disputes or for disputes below a specified threshold. Binding expert determination is not acceptable as a stand-alone dispute resolution mechanism, although it may be acceptable as a preliminary step in a tiered dispute resolution clause (e.g., expert determination for valuation disputes, with unresolved disputes escalated to LCIA arbitration).

491: **[12.1 --- When Escalation Is Required]{.underline}**
492:

Proposals that fall within those ranges may be agreed by the desk lead (at Director level) without reference to the Credit Committee. Proposals that fall outside those ranges --- but within the escalation band --- require Credit Committee approval before they may be agreed.

498: >
499: > \(b\) Corporate haircuts below 4.0%. Note: the 3.5%--4.0% band is a grey zone; escalate if the counterparty proposes any haircut below 4.0%, even if the proposed haircut is above the 3.5% walk-away threshold.

501: > \(c\) Any margin threshold above \$500,000 for either party (Buyer or Seller).
502: >
503: > \(d\) Cross-default thresholds between \$25,000,001 and \$50,000,000.

505: > \(e\) Act of Insolvency grace periods between 16 and 20 business days. Note: above 20 business days is a firm walk-away regardless of Credit Committee view.

507: > \(f\) Any deviation from English governing law. This is both an escalation trigger and a walk-away; the Credit Committee may consider the matter but is not expected to approve any deviation from English law.

509: > \(g\) Any modification to the Net Exposure Cap set by the Credit Committee for a specific counterparty. The Net Exposure Cap is a Credit Committee-set parameter; the desk does not have authority to modify it, even within a narrow range.

511: > \(h\) Acceptance of exclusive court jurisdiction (of any court, in any jurisdiction).
512: >
513: > \(i\) Any non-standard netting, set-off, or close-out netting provisions --- including any provisions that modify the close-out netting mechanics of Paragraph 10 of the GMRA, any provisions that introduce a set-off right that is broader than the GMRA\'s standard set-off provisions, or any provisions that restrict the Non-Defaulting Party\'s right to calculate a Default Market Value.

517: **[12.2 --- Escalation Procedure]{.underline}**
518: 
519: The escalation procedure is as follows:
520: 
521: 1\. The desk lead (currently Henrik J. Lindqvist for the London Branch) prepares a **one-page deviation memorandum** setting out:
522: 
523: > \(a\) the Voss Bank preferred position on the relevant term;
524: >
525: > \(b\) the counterparty\'s proposal, including the specific language proposed (with a redline against the Voss Bank position where applicable);
526: >
527: > \(c\) the commercial rationale for the deviation --- i.e., why the counterparty is insisting on a position outside the acceptable range, and whether there are offsetting commercial benefits (e.g., improved pricing, higher volumes, or concessions on other terms);
528: >
529: > \(d\) any risk-mitigating conditions proposed --- i.e., additional protections that Voss Bank could negotiate to offset the increased risk of the deviation (e.g., a lower Net Exposure Cap, enhanced reporting obligations, additional collateral requirements, or a shorter tenor limit).

531: 2\. The memorandum is submitted to the Credit Committee via the **Zürich Legal Coordination inbox** (legalcoord@vossbank.ch). The memorandum should be marked \"GMRA Deviation --- \[Counterparty Name\] --- \[Term\]\" in the subject line.

533: 3\. **Target turnaround:** 3 business days for standard deviations; 1 business day for time-sensitive negotiations (e.g., where a Turn deadline is imminent or where the counterparty has set a deadline for commercial agreement). If the desk requires expedited turnaround, this should be noted in the subject line of the submission email.

535: 4\. The Credit Committee will respond with one of three decisions: (i) approved as proposed; (ii) approved with conditions (specifying risk-mitigating conditions that must be incorporated into the GMRA); or (iii) declined (in which case the desk must revert to the preferred position or the nearest acceptable position within the playbook range).

553: **[Section 13 --- Income Payments]{.underline}**
554: 
555: **[13.1 --- Standard Position]{.underline}**
556: 
557: Manufactured Payments on Purchased Securities --- that is, payments by the Buyer to the Seller equal to the income (e.g., coupon payments, interest distributions) that the Seller would have received on the Purchased Securities had those securities not been transferred to the Buyer --- are due on the **next business day** following the record date for the relevant income payment.
558: 
559: This timing convention ensures that the manufactured payment is made promptly after the record date, without the settlement risk that would arise if the payment were aligned with the actual distribution date (which may fall on a weekend, public holiday, or non-business day in the relevant settlement system).
560: 
561: **[13.2 --- Negotiation Guidance]{.underline}**
562: 
563: The desk should resist counterparty attempts to align manufactured payment dates with actual payment dates (which may fall on non-business days and create settlement risk). The \"next business day following the record date\" convention is standard market practice for GMRA manufactured payments and should not be controversial with most counterparties.
564: 
565: If a counterparty proposes an alternative timing convention --- for example, manufactured payments due on the actual payment date, or manufactured payments due on the second business day following the record date --- the desk should explain that the standard convention is designed to minimise settlement risk and operational complexity, and should insist on the standard position.
566: 
567: The desk should also ensure that the GMRA clearly specifies the obligations of both parties with respect to manufactured payments in the context of a margin transfer. If Margin Securities have been delivered, the obligation to make manufactured payments on those Margin Securities should be addressed separately from the obligation to make manufactured payments on Purchased Securities.

593: **[Section 15 --- FINMA Regulatory Requirements]{.underline}**
594: 
595: **[15.1 --- Close-Out Netting Opinions]{.underline}**
596: 
597: Prior to executing any GMRA, Legal must confirm that a current (within 12 months) enforceability opinion on close-out netting under the laws of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction is on file. The opinion must be provided by a law firm approved by Voss Bank\'s Chief Legal Officer and must cover the following matters:
598: 
599: > • The enforceability of the GMRA\'s close-out netting provisions (Paragraph 10) under the laws of the counterparty\'s jurisdiction of organisation.
600: >
601: > • The enforceability of close-out netting in the event of the counterparty\'s insolvency, including any applicable insolvency safe harbours or exemptions.
602: >
603: > • For US counterparties, the opinion must specifically address SIPA/SIPC treatment of repo collateral and the enforceability of netting under the US Bankruptcy Code safe harbours (11 U.S.C. §§ 559, 561, and related provisions). The opinion must confirm that repo transactions under the GMRA qualify as \"repurchase agreements\" for the purposes of the Bankruptcy Code safe harbours and that the Non-Defaulting Party\'s contractual right to liquidate, terminate, or accelerate is protected from the automatic stay.
604: 
605: The netting opinion must be refreshed at least annually (i.e., a new opinion must be obtained within 12 months of the date of the most recent opinion). If a netting opinion is more than 12 months old at the time of execution of a new GMRA or at the time of entry into a new Transaction under an existing GMRA, the desk must not proceed until a refreshed opinion is obtained.
606: 
607: Legal maintains a register of all netting opinions on file, including the jurisdiction, the date of the opinion, the opining law firm, and the expiry date. The desk should check this register before commencing any new GMRA negotiation.
608: 
609: **[15.2 --- Capital Treatment]{.underline}**
610: 
611: The GMRA must include terms sufficient to ensure that reverse repo transactions qualify for securities financing transaction (SFT) treatment under the Basel III framework as implemented by FINMA (Capital Adequacy Ordinance (CAO), Art. 56 et seq.). SFT treatment allows Voss Bank to recognise the collateral received under reverse repo transactions for the purposes of calculating credit risk-weighted assets and leverage ratio exposure, subject to compliance with the applicable eligibility conditions.
612: 
613: Key conditions for SFT treatment include:
614: 
615: > • The GMRA must provide for enforceable close-out netting (see Section 15.1).
616: >
617: > • The collateral must be revalued at least daily (which is ensured by the GMRA\'s standard margin maintenance provisions).
618: >
619: > • The collateral must be liquid and must not exhibit a material positive correlation with the credit quality of the counterparty (this is ensured by the Eligible Collateral criteria set out in Section 3).
620: 
621: Haircuts below HQLA floors (see Section 3.3) may cause the transaction to attract higher capital charges under the standardised approach supervisory haircut framework. If haircuts approach the HQLA floors, the desk must escalate to Treasury (Zürich) to confirm the capital impact before agreeing the haircut level.
622: 
623: **[15.3 --- Large Exposure Reporting]{.underline}**
624: 
625: Aggregate gross exposure to a single counterparty under the GMRA must be monitored against FINMA large exposure limits. Under the FINMA framework, a bank\'s total exposure to a single counterparty (or group of connected counterparties) may not exceed 25% of the bank\'s eligible capital (Tier 1 capital plus Tier 2 capital, subject to applicable limits).
626: 
627: The Net Exposure Cap set by the Credit Committee for each counterparty is designed to remain well within the FINMA large exposure limit, providing a buffer against fluctuations in exposure due to market movements, new trades, or collateral value changes. The desk should be aware that the Net Exposure Cap is not the same as the large exposure limit --- the Cap is typically set at a level significantly below the regulatory limit to allow headroom for operational and market-driven exposure increases.
628: 
629: If the aggregate gross exposure to a counterparty under the GMRA approaches the Net Exposure Cap, or if the desk becomes aware of circumstances that could cause the aggregate exposure to exceed the FINMA large exposure limit (including exposure under other master agreements, such as the ISDA Master Agreement), the desk must immediately notify Risk Management (Zürich) and the Credit Committee.
